title: Modi's December Canada Visit Is Set to Move Ties in a New Direction
excerpt: Jaishankar and Anand call the December 11-12 visit a "building block" as analyst Vina Nadjibulla argues the India-Canada reset must go beyond trade and rebuild trust on the security track too.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada on December 11 and 12, with stops in Toronto and Ottawa, the Indian High Commission in Ottawa said on October 16 — a date Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also confirmed.
  • External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, meeting in Atlanta on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, agreed the visit will be another "building block" in the two countries' relationship.
  • Analyst Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, argues the reset must go beyond trade: trust is still lagging political momentum, and the security track must show credible progress alongside the economic one.
  • For Canada's large Indian diaspora, what to watch is concrete: whether the visit produces a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) announcement and visible progress on the security dialogue that followed the 2023 rupture.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Canada in December is set to move India-Canada ties in a new direction, after three years in which the relationship was defined by rupture. Jaishankar met Anand in Atlanta on Friday, on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, and the two assessed what an official statement called the "steady growth" in cooperation. They agreed, the statement said, that Modi's visit will be another "building block" in the two countries' ambitious relationship, and agreed to stay in close contact ahead of it.

The dates are already public. On October 16, the Indian High Commission in Ottawa said Modi will visit Canada on December 11 and 12. Carney confirmed the dates, saying he had spoken to Modi and the visit will take place in Toronto and Ottawa. Earlier this month, during her visit to India, Anand met Modi and said they had a productive discussion on strengthening ties in trade, technology and energy.

How the rupture happened — and how the reset was built

India-Canada relations hit rock bottom after then Prime Minister Justin Trudeau alleged in 2023 a potential Indian link to the killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar. India dismissed the accusation as "absurd." Missions were downsized and High Commissioners sent back. Carney's victory in the parliamentary election in April last year helped rebuild relations, the two countries agreed to revive several mechanisms, and ties have seen a major upswing since Carney's visit to India in March, when the two prime ministers set out a road map in a joint statement.

Below the official level, unofficial diplomacy kept channels open during the freeze. In a conversation with India's World, Vina Nadjibulla described Track 2 work — former diplomats, business leaders, academics, think-tank experts, people from the security community and civil society — whose first priority was to ensure the rupture did not become a complete breakdown. A first dialogue in New Delhi in February 2025 discussed restoring diplomatic representation, resuming trade discussions, creating dedicated security channels and rebuilding public trust; by a second dialogue in Ottawa in October 2025, the question had shifted to making the reset durable.

"Track 2 can keep the door from being permanently locked. Political leadership still has to decide to open it."

— Vina Nadjibulla, Centre for Strategic Statecraft

Two tracks, and the trust question

Nadjibulla argues the reset is proceeding on two parallel tracks. The diplomatic and economic track is visible — ministerial visits, trade negotiations, commercial agreements. The security and law enforcement track is less visible but active, with a regular NSA-level dialogue on organised crime, extremism, foreign interference and transnational repression. She calls that approach fundamentally right, but warns the tracks cannot become disconnected, and that Ottawa should explain publicly what its security engagement has actually achieved.

She also describes US President Donald Trump as an accelerator, not the architect, of the reset: Canada has energy, uranium, critical minerals, food, capital, AI and aerospace capabilities, while India brings scale, technology and engineering talent, a rapidly expanding market and growing industrial capacity — plus deep people-to-people connections. Both governments, she notes, are aiming to conclude accelerated CEPA negotiations by the end of the year.

What to watch in December

The December 11-12 visit is the next test. The concrete markers are a CEPA announcement, commercial deals, and whether either government says publicly what has changed on the security concerns that drove the rupture. As the report of the Jaishankar-Anand meeting put it, the ministers themselves framed the visit as a building block — the question Nadjibulla poses is whether the blocks are being laid on trust that can withstand the next serious disagreement.
